title: Massage Gun Buying Guide: What Actually Matters
excerpt: Cut through the marketing hype. Learn which specs matter and which don't when shopping for a percussion massager.
content:
# Massage Gun Buying Guide: What Actually Matters

The massage gun market is saturated with devices ranging from $30 Amazon specials to $600 professional-grade units. After testing 23 models, here's what you actually need to know.

## The Three Specs That Matter

### 1. Stall Force (40+ lbs)
Stall force measures how much pressure the device can handle before the motor stops. Anything under 40 lbs will struggle with tight muscles. Our top picks deliver 50-60 lbs.

### 2. Noise Level (Under 50 dB)
If you live in an apartment or plan to use your massage gun while others are home, noise matters. Quality devices operate at 38-48 dB—about as loud as a quiet conversation.

### 3. Battery Life (2+ hours)
Look for at least 2 hours of runtime. This gives you 8-12 sessions between charges at typical 10-15 minute usage periods.

## Specs That Don't Matter

**RPM claims**: Manufacturers inflate these numbers. 2400-3200 RPM is plenty.

**Number of attachments**: You'll use 2-3 heads regularly. More heads = more to lose.

**"Smart" features**: App connectivity adds complexity without meaningful benefit.

## Price Sweet Spot

The $200-$350 range delivers the best performance-to-value ratio. Budget models under $150 often lack power and durability. Premium models over $400 offer marginal improvements.

## Our Top Picks by Use Case

- **Best Overall**: Theragun Prime ($299) - Quiet, powerful, 2-year warranty
- **Best Value**: Ekrin Athletics B37 ($199) - Solid specs, no frills
- **Most Portable**: Hyperice Hypervolt Go 2 ($159) - Compact, TSA-friendly

## Testing Methodology

We measure stall force with calibrated scales, noise levels with professional dB meters at 1m distance, and battery life through controlled discharge cycles.

All devices tested on large muscle groups (quads, calves, back) across multiple body types.

## Final Thoughts

A massage gun should be quiet enough for apartment use, powerful enough for deep tissue work, and reliable enough to last years. Focus on stall force, noise, and build quality—everything else is marketing.
